title: Word Problems & Translation
weightage: High — translation underlies a large share of GRE algebra, rates, and Data Interpretation questions
intro: Most GRE Quant questions do not arrive as equations — they arrive as sentences, and the real skill is translation: turning words into algebra you can solve. The arithmetic is usually easy; the points are won or lost in the setup. Define your variable explicitly ("let n be the number of adult tickets"), convert each phrase into a symbol as you read, and the equation almost writes itself. A quiet but decisive habit is to name the variable for the quantity the question actually asks about, so you are not left solving for the wrong thing at the end. This chapter drills the four highest-frequency families: general word-to-algebra translation, ages and consecutive integers, interest and growth, and the discipline of setting up equations cleanly. Because the on-screen calculator is basic, the winning approach is to model carefully and keep the numbers small — and on many GRE items, plugging in the answer choices or testing smart numbers beats solving from scratch.

topics.name: Translating Words to Algebra
topics.details: Translation is a word-by-word conversion. A handful of keywords map to operations: "is" means equals, "of" (with a fraction or percent) means multiply, "sum"/"more than"/"increased by" mean add, "difference"/"less than"/"fewer than" mean subtract, and "per"/"for each" signal division or a rate. The one phrase that trips everyone is "less than": "5 less than x" is x − 5, not 5 − x — the order flips. Start by writing "let x = …" for the unknown you want, express every other quantity in terms of it, then turn the sentence's main "is/equals" into an equals sign. Read the final question again before answering: a problem may make you solve for x but ask for 2x + 1. On the GRE, when the numbers are answer choices, it is often faster to plug a choice back into the words and check than to solve the equation forward — the choices are a resource, not just an endpoint.

solved.problem: Translate and solve: "7 more than twice a number is 23."
solved.solution: Let the number be x. "Twice a number" = 2x; "7 more than" it = 2x + 7; "is 23" gives 2x + 7 = 23. Then 2x = 16, x = 8.

solved.problem: Translate: "5 less than three times a number equals the number increased by 7." Find the number.
solved.solution: Let x be the number: 3x − 5 = x + 7. So 2x = 12, x = 6. (Note "5 less than 3x" is 3x − 5, not 5 − 3x.)

solved.problem: A number is 40% of 150. What is the number?
The sum of a number and its double is 27. Find the number.
solved.solution: Let the number be x. x + 2x = 27, so 3x = 27 and x = 9.

unsolved.problem: "4 more than half a number is 19." Find the number.
"8 less than a number is 12." Find the number.

A number increased by 25% of itself equals 75. Find the number.
The sum of a number and 12 is three times the number. Find it.

topics.name: Ages & Consecutive Integers
topics.details: Age and consecutive-integer problems are translation with a time or sequence twist. For ages, define the present ages first, then adjust for time: "5 years ago" subtracts 5 from every person's current age, and "in 8 years" adds 8 to each — the mistake to avoid is adjusting only one person. For consecutive integers, model them as n, n + 1, n + 2, …; consecutive even or odd integers step by 2, as n, n + 2, n + 4. A useful GRE fact: the sum of an odd count of consecutive integers equals the middle term times the count, so three consecutive integers summing to 72 have middle term 24 (giving 23, 24, 25) — you can often skip the algebra entirely. Keep track of who or what each variable represents; these problems punish a variable you defined loosely more than they punish arithmetic.

solved.problem: The sum of three consecutive integers is 72. Find them.
solved.solution: Let them be n, n + 1, n + 2. Sum = 3n + 3 = 72, so 3n = 69, n = 23. The integers are 23, 24, 25. (Middle term = 72/3 = 24 confirms it.)

solved.problem: Maria is 4 years older than Sam. In 6 years the sum of their ages will be 40. How old is Sam now?
solved.solution: Let Sam = s, Maria = s + 4. In 6 years: (s + 6) + (s + 4 + 6) = 40, so 2s + 16 = 40, 2s = 24, s = 12.

solved.problem: The sum of two consecutive even integers is 46. Find them.
solved.solution: Let them be n and n + 2. 2n + 2 = 46, so 2n = 44, n = 22. The integers are 22 and 24.

solved.problem: A father is three times as old as his son. In 12 years he will be twice as old. Find the son's current age.
solved.solution: Let son = s, father = 3s. In 12 years: 3s + 12 = 2(s + 12), so 3s + 12 = 2s + 24, giving s = 12.

unsolved.problem: The sum of three consecutive integers is 90. Find the largest.
Two consecutive odd integers sum to 56. Find them.
Ravi is 5 years younger than Priya. Their ages sum to 33. How old is Ravi?
A mother is 4 times as old as her daughter. In 20 years she will be twice as old. Find the daughter's age now.
The sum of four consecutive integers is 90. Find the smallest.

topics.name: Interest & Growth
topics.details: Interest and growth problems are translation applied to money and populations over time. Simple interest adds the same amount every period: I = P · r · t, where P is the principal, r the rate as a decimal, and t the time — so $2,000 at 5% for 3 years earns 2000 × 0.05 × 3 = $300. Compound interest instead multiplies each period: A = P(1 + r)ᵗ, so the same $2,000 at 5% compounded annually for 3 years grows to 2000 × 1.05³. Over the same terms, compound always yields more than simple, and the GRE loves a Quantitative Comparison contrasting the two. Population, depreciation, and "increases by x% each year" problems use the same compound multiplier — a decrease just makes the multiplier (1 − r). Keep the rate as a decimal and, since the basic on-screen calculator will not do exponents, expect small time periods (t = 2 or 3) so you can multiply the factor out by hand.

solved.problem: Find the simple interest on $1,500 at 6% per year for 4 years.
$1,000 is compounded annually at 10% for 2 years. Find the final amount.
A town of 8,000 grows 5% per year. What is its population after 2 years?
Quantitative Comparison. $1,000 for 2 years at 10% per year. Quantity A: total value under annual compounding. Quantity B: total value under simple interest. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Compound: 1000 × 1.21 = $1,210. Simple: 1000 + 1000 × 0.10 × 2 = $1,200. Quantity A is greater — compounding always beats simple over more than one period.

unsolved.problem: Simple interest on $2,500 at 4% for 3 years?
$5,000 compounded annually at 20% for 2 years — final amount?
A $12,000 car depreciates 10% per year. Its value after 2 years?

topics.name: Setting Up Equations
topics.details: The hardest part of a multi-quantity word problem is the setup, not the solving. When two unknowns are related, express both in terms of a single variable so you end with one equation — for a mixture of adult and child tickets, let a be the number of adult tickets and (total − a) be the child tickets, rather than juggling two letters. When the relationships genuinely need two variables, write a system and use substitution or elimination. Always attach units and a clear definition to each variable; a labelled "let x = number of nickels" prevents the classic coin-problem error of confusing the count of coins with their monetary value. Check the answer against the sentence, not just the algebra — a value that solves the equation but gives a negative count or a fractional person signals a setup slip. And remember the GRE-specific shortcut: with numeric answer choices, back-solving (testing a choice in the original wording) is frequently faster and less error-prone than building and solving the equation.

solved.problem: Tickets cost $8 (adult) and $5 (child). 30 tickets sold for $198 total. How many adult tickets?
solved.solution: Let a = adult tickets, so child = 30 − a. Value: 8a + 5(30 − a) = 198 → 8a + 150 − 5a = 198 → 3a = 48 → a = 16.

solved.problem: A jar has nickels and dimes, 20 coins worth $1.35. How many dimes? (nickel = $0.05, dime = $0.10)
The length of a rectangle is 3 more than twice its width, and the perimeter is 36. Find the width.
solved.solution: Let w = width, length = 2w + 3. Perimeter 2(w + 2w + 3) = 36 → 2(3w + 3) = 36 → 3w + 3 = 18 → w = 5.

solved.problem: A 40-liter mixture is 25% acid. How many liters of acid must be added to make it 40% acid?

unsolved.problem: $6 and $10 tickets, 25 sold for $186. How many $6 tickets?
Pens cost $2, notebooks $5. 12 items cost $39. How many notebooks?

shortcuts: Translate as you read: "is" → =, "of" → ×, "more than" → +, "less than" → −, "per" → ÷. Convert each phrase the moment you meet it.
"Less than" flips the order: "5 less than x" is x − 5, never 5 − x. This single sign trap is the most common translation error.
For an odd count of consecutive integers, the sum equals the middle term times the count — so three summing to 72 have middle term 24 with no algebra.
Express two related unknowns with ONE variable (adult a, child = total − a) so you solve one equation instead of a system.
Compound growth uses the multiplier (1 + r) per period; a decrease uses (1 − r). Chain it for small t rather than reaching for exponent keys.
With numeric answer choices, back-solve: drop a choice into the original wording and check. It often beats solving forward and dodges algebra slips.
mistakes: Reversing "less than" or "subtracted from" — the order of the two terms flips.
Adjusting only one person's age for "in 5 years" instead of every age in the problem.
Confusing the COUNT of coins with their monetary VALUE in coin problems.
Solving for the variable but forgetting the question asked for a different expression (e.g. 2x + 1, not x).
Using compound-interest arithmetic where the problem says simple interest, or vice versa.
Leaving a rate as a whole number (5 instead of 0.05) inside I = P·r·t or the growth factor.

pyq.q: A GRE word problem gives numeric answer choices. What is the fastest reliable tactic?
pyq.a: Back-solve: substitute a choice into the original sentence and check whether it fits. Starting from a middle choice narrows it in one or two tries, and it sidesteps setup errors entirely.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — $1,000 invested for 2 years at 8%. Quantity A: value under annual compounding. Quantity B: value under simple interest. Which is greater?
pyq.a: Compound = 1000 × 1.08² = 1166.40; simple = 1000 + 160 = 1160. Quantity A is greater — compounding beats simple beyond one period.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry — the sum of three consecutive integers is 84. Enter the largest.
pyq.a: Middle term = 84/3 = 28, so the integers are 27, 28, 29 and the largest is 29. Use the middle-term shortcut instead of solving 3n + 3 = 84.

pyq.q: A mixture problem asks how much of one component to add. What stays fixed and what changes?
pyq.a: Track the amount of the target substance and the total volume separately: adding pure acid changes both numerator and denominator; adding water changes only the total. Set the new ratio equal to the target percent.

flashcards.back: middle term × count (e.g. three summing to 72 → middle 24).
I = P · r · t (same amount added each period).
A = P(1 + r)ᵗ; decrease uses (1 − r).
Adjust EVERY person's age by ∓t, not just one.
Write both with one variable (e.g. total − x) to get a single equation.

summary: GRE word problems are won in translation, not arithmetic. Convert phrases to symbols as you read ("is" = equals, "of" = times, "less than" flips the order), and always define your variable for the quantity actually asked. Model the classic families directly: consecutive integers as n, n + 1, n + 2 (using the middle-term sum shortcut), ages by adjusting every person for time, and money by choosing simple interest (I = P·r·t) or compound growth (P(1 + r)ᵗ) as the wording demands. For multi-quantity setups, express two unknowns with one variable, keep units attached, and sanity-check the answer against the sentence. Above all, remember the GRE gift of numeric answer choices: back-solving from the choices is frequently the fastest, safest route to the point.
